idiom_name: ActiveRecord::Base subclass (table and columns inferred from the class name)
implementation_notes: This is the pattern's namesake home: subclass ActiveRecord::Base (ApplicationRecord), let the pluralised class name select the table, get one attribute per column without declaring them, and persist through instance save/update/destroy, with validations, callbacks, associations and migrations supplied by the framework. What replaces the classic structure is convention over configuration plus a schema read at boot: the mapping is never written down. Choose it when the application is Rails; the cost is that the mapping is implicit, so schema and behaviour are discovered from the same class.
code_sketch:
class Book < ApplicationRecord
  validates :title, presence: true
end

book = Book.new(title: "The Hobbit")
book.save!                                        # INSERT
book.update(title: "There and Back Again")        # UPDATE
Book.where(author: "Tolkien").first               # finder
book.destroy
pitfalls: save returns false on validation failure while save! raises: silently dropping the false loses the write, and callbacks that mutate state run in both cases.
The whole changed attribute set is written on save and there is no optimistic locking unless lock_version exists, so concurrent edits overwrite each other by default.
Association access in loops hits the database per row; includes/preload are the fix, and the record class gives no hint that it is happening.

variants.name: Sequel::Model (toolkit, explicit dataset)
variants.idiom_name: Sequel::Model subclass with an explicit dataset and plugin set
variants.implementation_notes: Sequel implements the same pattern outside Rails and makes the mapping explicit: the model class is bound to a dataset (Sequel::Model(:books) or set_dataset), instances carry save (which creates or updates the record), update, save_changes (changed columns only) and destroy, and behaviour is added by plugins instead of a framework's implicit magic. What replaces the classic structure is a dataset plus a plugin list, so nothing about the table is guessed from the class name. Choose it when you want record objects but not Rails, or when an existing schema does not follow Rails naming conventions.
variants.code_sketch:
class Book < Sequel::Model(:books)
  plugin :validation_helpers
end

book = Book.new(title: "The Hobbit")
book.save                       # INSERT
book.update(title: "There and Back Again")
book.save_changes               # UPDATE of changed columns only
Book.where(author: "Tolkien").first
pitfalls: The dataset must be set before the class body runs when you use the Sequel::Model(:table) shorthand; a bare Sequel::Model defined first throws on first access.
save_changes skips save hooks and validation unless they are run explicitly, which surprises code migrated from ActiveRecord's save.
Strict parameter checking raises on unknown setters; mass-assigning a request hash needs set_fields or an explicit whitelist.
